title: Least-to-Most Prompting
description: Decompose a complex problem into a sequence of simpler sub-problems and solve them in order, feeding each solution as context for the next. Achieves generalisation on problems that defeat standard Chain-of-Thought.
body: Least-to-Most Prompting Description Least-to-Most Prompting (Zhou et al., 2022) solves complex tasks by first asking the model to break the problem into an ordered list of sub-problems (easiest first), then solving each one sequentially, appending each answer to the context before tackling the next. The key insight: if the model can solve every sub-problem, composing the answers gives the final solution. This overcomes CoT failures where the model attempts to solve everything at once and loses track of intermediate steps. On SCAN compositionality tasks, Least-to-Most achieved 99.7% accuracy versus CoT's 16%. It also significantly outperforms CoT on DROP and math word problems with multiple constraints. body: Meta-Prompting Description Meta-Prompting (Zhang et al., 2024) operates at the prompt-construction level rather than the answer level. A meta-model receives a task description and generates the optimal prompt (or a set of candidate prompts) for a task model to execute. This creates a two-level hierarchy: 1. Meta-level: "Given this task, what is the best prompt to give a model to solve it?" 2. Task-level: The generated prompt is executed by the task model. In production, meta-prompting is used in AutoGen's system message generation, Semantic Kernel's planner, and DSPy's optimizer. When to Use - You have a diverse set of task types and can't hand-craft prompts for each. - You want automatic prompt adaptation to user intent at runtime. - Building multi-agent systems where agent prompts should specialise per task. - Don't use when task distribution is narrow and fixed prompts are optimal. title: Self-Consistency
description: Sample N independent reasoning chains for the same question and majority-vote the final answer. Trades cost for accuracy Ã¢ÂÂ robust on math and logic, surprisingly cheap with smaller-than-frontier models.
body: Self-Consistency Description Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) augments Chain of Thought by sampling N independent reasoning chains at temperature > 0, parsing each one's final answer, and majority-voting. Wrong reasoning chains tend to scatter across many wrong answers; correct reasoning converges. So the modal answer is usually the right one. It's the simplest "test-time compute" trick that exists, and it works. On GSM8K-style arithmetic, self-consistency typically lifts accuracy by 5Ã¢ÂÂ15 points over single-shot CoT at the cost of ~NÃÂ tokens. When to Use - The task has a single, parseable final answer (math, logic, multiple-choice, classification). - You can afford NÃÂ cost (typically 5). - You don't have access to a reasoning-tuned model that already does this implicitly. - Don't use when the answer is open-ended text Ã¢ÂÂ voting is meaningless on prose. title: Step-Back Prompting
description: Prompt the LLM to first answer a high-level abstraction (the 'step-back' question) before solving the original task. Improves performance on multi-step reasoning by grounding the answer in principles before details.
body: Step-Back Prompting Description Step-Back Prompting (Zheng et al., 2023) instructs the model to first retrieve a high-level principle or concept relevant to the question before attempting a solution. The two-step structure is: 1. Step-back question: "What is the general principle or concept behind this problem?" 2. Grounded answer: Use the retrieved principle as context for the original answer. On MMLU (physics, chemistry) and TimeQA benchmarks, Step-Back Prompting improved accuracy by 7-27% over direct prompting and 1-11% over Chain-of-Thought. When to Use - Multi-hop questions requiring domain knowledge before specific calculation. - Research agents that need to ground answers in principles before synthesis. - RAG pipelines where the retrieval query benefits from abstraction before specifics. - Don't use for simple factual lookups or purely procedural tasks with no principles. body: Perceptual Image Hashing Category: Multimodal Level: intermediate Stability: experimental Version: v1 Description Byte hashes cannot recognize the same picture after a resize or re-encode. A perceptual hash captures visual structure: downsample to a fixed grid, threshold each cell against the grid mean, and pack the bits into a fixed-width fingerprint. Face or semantic similarity is out of scope; this is structural near-duplicate detection. body: Iframe Handling Category: Web Level: intermediate Stability: experimental Version: v1 Description Iframe handling turns a flat page into a tree of documents. The skill covers enumerating frames, resolving the target frame by identity rather than by selector alone, re-scoping lookups to the frame document, and proving the current scope before and after every action. The core discipline is that a selector never identifies an element on its own in a framed page; a (frame, selector) pair does. When to Use Use when a target page embeds content in one or more iframes: embedded forms, payment widgets, media players, sandboxed previews, or third-party embeds that must be automated or audited. Do not assume a single flat DOM. The same selector can resolve in several frames, and acting inside the wrong frame produces plausible-looking but incorrect results. title: "Infinite Scroll Handling"
description: Extract complete data sets from pages that reveal content incrementally on scroll, with termination detection, batch deduplication, and bounded run budgets.
body: Infinite Scroll Handling Category: Web Level: basic Stability: experimental Version: v1 Description Infinite scroll pages never announce that they are finished. The skill treats scrolling as a batch protocol: extract the visible viewport, scroll one viewport height, wait for the page to settle, deduplicate against what is already collected, and terminate on a budget, a sentinel element, or a run of empty batches. Each batch is persisted as it arrives so a late failure loses only the tail. When to Use Use when a feed, gallery, or results list reveals content as the user scrolls and the full set must be collected rather than sampled. Do not scroll until the page stops by itself without a hard budget. Some feeds generate content forever and will exhaust memory, time, or rate limits before they exhaust content. title: "Cohort Analysis"
description: Segment records into cohorts by a shared anchor event, measure retention and behavior across periods, and compare cohort trajectories with explicit handling of censoring and cohort size.
body: Cohort Analysis Category: Data Level: basic Stability: experimental Version: v1 Description Cohort analysis compares groups defined by when they started, not by who they are. The skill covers assigning entities to cohorts by their first anchor event, binning cohorts by the calendar rule, computing period-by-period retention relative to cohort size, and censoring the trailing periods where not enough time has elapsed to observe the window. Comparisons are always normalized rates with cohort sizes attached, never raw counts. When to Use Use when behavior must be compared across groups defined by a starting event: signup month, first purchase, activation week, or onboarding batch. Do not compare raw counts across cohorts of different sizes. Normalize to rates and report cohort sizes alongside every comparison.
